messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

As a paramedic, Amir had seen his fair share of gruesome injuries, but nothing could have prepared him for the day his younger brother, Ali, was rushed to the hospital with severe burns covering most of his body. The memory of that day still felt like it was etched into his mind, as vivid and alive as if it had happened yesterday. He recalled the smell of antiseptic wafting through the air, the sound of beeping machines, and the sight of Ali's charred skin - a visual that haunted him to this day. The months following the accident were a blur for Amir. He threw himself into work, taking on extra shifts and trying to keep his mind occupied with the demands of being a paramedic. But every time he responded to an emergency call involving severe injuries, the memories came flooding back. The sight of visible wounds or burns would transport him right back to that hospital room, reliving the terror and helplessness he felt as he watched his brother fight for his life. As time went on, Amir began to avoid certain aspects of his job, opting out of shifts in the ER or anywhere else he might encounter patients with severe injuries. He couldn't bear the thought of being confronted with those visual triggers again, fearing it would send him spiraling back into that dark place. His colleagues started to notice a change in him - he was more withdrawn, less confident in his abilities. But Amir just shrugged it off, telling them he was fine, that he just needed some time to recharge. But the truth was, Amir wasn't fine. He was struggling to concentrate, finding himself zoning out in meetings or while driving. Simple tasks became overwhelming, and he would often find himself jumping at the slightest touch, his heart racing as if he was back in that hospital room, waiting for news about Ali's condition. He started choosing seats in public places based on how safe they felt - near exits, with a clear view of the surroundings. At home, Amir's wife noticed the change in him too. He would get agitated at the smallest things, and when she tried to talk to him about it, he would shut down, telling her he just needed some space. But deep down, Amir was consumed by feelings of guilt and inadequacy. He couldn't shake the thought that he had failed Ali in some way, that he should have been able to protect him from harm. As the memories continued to haunt him, Amir began to withdraw further into himself. He stopped socializing with friends, stopped going out, stopped living. His wife tried to reach out to him, but he just pushed her away, too afraid to let her see the broken person he felt like inside. And yet, despite all this, Amir couldn't bring himself to seek help. He was convinced that he was permanently damaged, that he would never be able to go back to being the person he once was. It wasn't until Ali's birthday, a few weeks ago, that Amir realized he needed help. He found himself breaking down in tears at work, unable to shake off the memories of that terrible day. Something inside him snapped, and for the first time, he acknowledged that he couldn't do this alone anymore. With a sense of trepidation, Amir made an appointment with a therapist, hoping against hope that someone could help him find his way back from the darkness that had consumed him.
